topic: Tự host TelltaleDNS trên VPS và Homelab: DNS chặn quảng cáo thế hệ mới, giải thích rõ từng truy vấn thay thế Pi-hole và AdGuard Home

repos.name: TelltaleDNS
repos.description: A small, fast DNS resolver and ad blocker that explains every answer. Per-device rules, encrypted DNS, and clustering across a Raspberry Pi and Kubernetes.

repos.name: Pi-hole
repos.description: A black hole for Internet advertisements

repos.name: AdGuard Home
repos.description: Network-wide ads & trackers blocking DNS server

notes.audience: Các lập trình viên, homelabber và quản trị viên VPS tại Việt Nam muốn tự host DNS server chặn quảng cáo hiệu năng cao, siêu nhẹ để thay thế hoặc nâng cấp từ Pi-hole và AdGuard Home.
notes.angle: TelltaleDNS là DNS sinkhole viết bằng Rust thế hệ mới: siêu nhẹ (14 MiB RAM), giải thích cặn kẽ từng truy vấn, cho phép giả lập thử rule trên traffic hôm qua và hỗ trợ cluster đồng bộ mượt mà giữa VPS và Pi.

facts.fact: TelltaleDNS giải thích rõ ràng lý do mỗi truy vấn được cho phép hoặc bị chặn tới từng danh sách và quy tắc cụ thể.
facts.quote: The query log says why each question was answered or blocked, which list and rule did it, and which upstream answered.

facts.fact: Cho phép chạy thử danh sách hoặc quy tắc chặn mới trên lưu lượng thực tế của ngày hôm trước để xem trước kết quả trước khi lưu.
facts.quote: You can run a new list or rule against yesterday's real traffic and see what it would have blocked before you save it.

facts.fact: Kích thước image chỉ khoảng 13 MiB, chạy không tải chỉ tốn khoảng 14 MiB RAM và lưu 1 triệu tên miền bị chặn trong 60 MiB bộ nhớ.
facts.quote: One static binary in an image of about 13 MiB, for amd64, arm64, and 32-bit Pi OS. It idles at about 14 MiB of memory, holds a million blocked names in 60 MiB

facts.fact: Đạt độ trễ phản hồi cực thấp: 99.999% phản hồi cache và chặn được gửi trong vòng 250 microsecond khi chịu tải từ máy khác.
facts.quote: sends 99.999 % of cached and blocked answers within 250 µs of the query arriving, under load from another machine

facts.fact: Tự phân giải đệ quy trực tiếp từ các DNS root server (recursive://) mà không cần phần mềm phụ như Unbound.
facts.quote: It filters with blocklists and per-device groups, and it can also resolve names itself from the root servers, so there is no second program to run.

facts.fact: Cố tình không tích hợp DHCP server; tự động nhận diện tên thiết bị thông qua router lease (UniFi, OPNsense) và mDNS.
facts.quote: No, on purpose. DHCP stays on your router or another server. TelltaleDNS reads device names from your router's lease list (UniFi and OPNsense) and from mDNS

facts.fact: Hỗ trợ gán định danh Client ID cho từng thiết bị trên các giao thức mã hóa DoT, DoH, DoH/3 và DoQ để phân nhóm rule.
facts.quote: Every encrypted listener (DoT, DoH, DoH over HTTP/3, and DoQ) takes a client ID: use https://dns.example.com/dns-query/kids-tablet, or the name kids-tablet.dns.example.com

facts.fact: Mô hình cluster DNS Active-Active không cần database ngoài, mỗi node lưu trữ dữ liệu nhúng riêng biệt.
facts.quote: No external database. Each node keeps its own small embedded store, so there is nothing shared to keep consistent. Answering DNS is active-active

facts.fact: Khi node chính hoặc Kubernetes gặp sự cố, các node khác vẫn tiếp tục phản hồi DNS từ cấu hình tốt gần nhất.
facts.quote: DNS keeps working. Every other node keeps answering from the last configuration it received, even after a restart.

facts.fact: Hỗ trợ công cụ import từ Pi-hole và Technitium; không có công cụ import AdGuard Home nhưng đọc được cú pháp danh sách của AdGuard.
facts.quote: the importers cover Pi-hole (telltale import pihole) and Technitium but not AdGuard Home, so you would add those lists again. Lists written in AdGuard syntax work as they are.

facts.fact: Mặc định xuất Prometheus metrics qua cổng 9153, giới hạn theo danh sách mạng được phép.
facts.quote: /metrics is served on port 9153 by default, limited to your allowed networks.

facts.fact: Khi triển khai container, cổng 53 yêu cầu Linux capability NET_BIND_SERVICE và chạy host network.
facts.quote: Port 53 needs NET_BIND_SERVICE: run as root with only that capability.

install: docker compose exec telltale telltale auth setup-token
caveats: Phần mềm đang ở giai đoạn pre-1.0, cấu hình và API có thể thay đổi giữa các phiên bản.
Không tích hợp DHCP server nội bộ, phải dựa vào router hoặc DHCP server bên ngoài.
Không có công cụ import tự động từ AdGuard Home (dù đọc được file danh sách cú pháp AdGuard).
Không thể chặn quảng cáo chia sẻ chung tên miền với nội dung chính như YouTube, Twitch, Facebook Ads (giới hạn cố hữu của chặn mức DNS).
Mặc định các truy vấn PTR (reverse DNS) cho IP mạng nội bộ trả về NXDOMAIN trừ khi được định tuyến thủ công về router.
Chưa hỗ trợ Dynamic DNS updates (RFC 2136) hoặc tự động dùng PTR để đặt tên cho thiết bị.
Cần chạy network_mode: host trên Docker để đọc đúng IP client và MAC của thiết bị.
Client ID trên DoH/DoT chỉ là định danh phân nhóm rule, không đóng vai trò mật khẩu xác thực (khi mở ra Internet cần kiểm soát IP hoặc qua VPN).
gaps: Giao diện Web UI hiện tại đã hỗ trợ tiếng Việt hay chưa?
Mức tiêu thụ tài nguyên thực tế khi gánh hàng nghìn truy vấn đồng thời trên gói VPS giá rẻ 1 vCPU 512MB RAM?
Làm thế nào để tích hợp gọn nhẹ với WireGuard hoặc Tailscale trên cùng một VPS mà không bị lộ cổng DNS ra Internet?
Hiệu năng định tuyến có điều kiện (conditional forwarding) tới các DNS ISP Việt Nam (Viettel, VNPT, FPT) để tối ưu ping khi chơi game ra sao?

## paimonsoror/telltaledns (https://github.com/paimonsoror/telltaledns)
Description: A small, fast DNS resolver and ad blocker that explains every answer. Per-device rules, encrypted DNS, and clustering across a Raspberry Pi and Kubernetes.
Homepage: https://paimonsoror.github.io/telltaledns/
Language: Rust; license: Apache-2.0; created 2026-10-03; last push 2026-11-16
Latest release: v0.7.0 (2026-11-16)
README (start):
# TelltaleDNS

[](https://github.com/paimonsoror/telltaledns/actions/workflows/ci.yml?query=branch%3Amain)
[](https://github.com/paimonsoror/telltaledns/security/code-scanning?query=branch%3Amain)
[](https://github.com/paimonsoror/telltaledns/releases/latest)
[](#license)
[](https://github.com/paimonsoror/telltaledns/pulls?q=is%3Apr+author%3Aapp%2Fdependabot)

**See every question. Answer on your terms.**

Every connection on your network starts with a DNS lookup. TelltaleDNS answers it in microseconds, filters it by your rules per device, and shows you exactly who asked, what they asked, and why it answered the way it did. It runs on a Raspberry Pi, in Kubernetes, or on both as one cluster that keeps answering even when parts of it fail.

> A *telltale* is the strip of yarn sailors tie to a sail to see what the wind is really doing. DNS is your network's telltale: it reveals what every device is up to.

  
    
    
  
  
  The dashboard on a demo network. Every device, name, and address in it is made up.

## Mission
Give everyone who runs a home or small network an honest, real-time view of what their devices are doing, and full control over it, without trading away speed, footprint, or reliability.

- **See:** every query is attributed to a device, explained, and timed per stage.
- **Decide:** your rules per device and group, enforced instantly at no performance cost.
- **Never fail:** DNS keeps answering from its last good config, whatever happens to the control plane.
- **Run anywhere:** the same artifact on a Pi, in a cluster, or both at once.

## What it does
- **Every answer explained.** The query log ties each query to a named device, times every stage, and says why it was answered that way. Names come from your router, from what devices announce over mDNS, or from the UI, and TelltaleDNS recognizes what each device is (a Roku player, a camera, a thermostat) from its maker and the names it asks for.
- **Your rules, per device.** Blocklists, groups for each network or VLAN, schedules, safe search, blocked services, rewrites, and quick rules. Before you save a change, see what it would have done to yesterday's real traffic.
- **Encrypted both ways.** DoT, DoH, and DoQ for your devices and to your upstreams, DNSSEC validation, and full recursion when you'd rather not forward at all.
- **Watch it work.** A dashboard for the whole cluster, one node, or one site. A heatmap of when your network asks, a flow from each group to its answers, answer times as a heatmap, every change marked on every chart, and which devices and names spent the error budget. Compare nodes side by side, see a device's rhythm and its day, and put it all on a wall display. Device anomalies and alerts; Prometheus metrics, OpenTelemetry, dnstap, and event sinks for your SIEM.
- **One cluster, many places.** A Pi and Kubernetes nodes share one config and one management plane. A witness lets a replica take over automatically, and the config can live in Git. Changes can reach a few canary nodes first and roll back by themselves if those start failing, and maintenance mode takes a node out of service without dropped queries or false alarms.
- **Private by design.** Privacy levels decide how much of each query is kept, from everything to counters only, and every change lands in an audit log.
- **Ready for agents.** A documented REST API with OpenAPI, `telltale ctl` for the shell, and MCP tools with plans and approval for AI agents.
- **Small and fast.** One static binary in an image of about 13 MiB, for amd64, arm64, and 32-bit Pi OS. It idles at about 14 MiB of memory, holds a million blocked names in 60 MiB, and sends 99.999 % of cached and blocked answers within 250 µs of the query arriving, under load from another machine ([measurements](docs/v1-gate.md)).
- **Verifiable.** Images are signed with cosign, each release binary carries its dependency list and an SBOM, and two builds of the same commit are identical ([how to check](docs/running.md#versions-and-updates)).

## Quick start
On a Raspberry Pi or any Linux host with Docker:
```sh
mkdir telltale && cd telltale
curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/paimonsoror/telltaledns/main/deploy/compose/compose.yaml
curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/paimonsoror/telltaledns/main/deploy/compose/telltale.toml
docker compose up -d
docker compose exec telltale telltale auth setup-token     # then open http://:8053/
```
Kubernetes (Helm), a native systemd install, clustering, and moving from Pi-hole or Technitium are covered in [`docs/running.md`](docs/running.md).

**Status:** pre-1.0. Tagged [releases](https://github.com/paimonsoror/telltaledns/releases) are stable (`latest`), and `edge` is built from every commit on `main`. Releases before 1.0 can still change configuration keys and APIs, and their notes call out every such change; the [roadmap](spec/10-roadmap-and-tasks.md) shows what's next. Project site: **https://paimonsoror.github.io/telltaledns/**

## AdguardTeam/AdGuardHome (https://github.com/AdguardTeam/AdGuardHome)
Description: Network-wide ads & trackers blocking DNS server
Homepage: https://adguard.com/adguard-home/overview.html
Language: TypeScript; license: GPL-3.0; created 2016-07-06; last push 2026-11-16
Latest release: v0.107.80 (2026-11-03)
README (start):
 

  
    
    
  

Privacy protection center for you and your devices

  Free and open source, powerful network-wide ads & trackers blocking DNS server.

  AdGuard.com |
  Wiki |
  Reddit |
  Twitter |
  Telegram
  
  
    
  
  
    
  
  
    
  
  
  
    
  
  
    
  

  

AdGuard Home is a network-wide software for blocking ads and tracking. After you set it up, it'll cover ALL your home devices, and you don't need any client-side software for that.

It operates as a DNS server that re-routes tracking domains to a “black hole”, thus preventing your devices from connecting to those servers. It's based on software we use for our public [AdGuard DNS] servers, and both share a lot of code.

## Getting Started

### Automated install (Linux/Unix/MacOS/FreeBSD/OpenBSD)

To install with `curl` run the following command:

```sh
curl -s -S -L https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AdguardTeam/AdGuardHome/master/scripts/install.sh | sh -s -- -v
```

To install with `wget` run the following command:

```sh
wget --no-verbose -O - https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AdguardTeam/AdGuardHome/master/scripts/install.sh | sh -s -- -v
```

To install with `fetch` run the following command:

```sh
fetch -o - https://raw.githubusercontent.com/AdguardTeam/AdGuardHome/master/scripts/install.sh | sh -s -- -v
```

The script also accepts some options:

- `-c ` to use specified channel;
- `-r` to reinstall AdGuard Home;
- `-u` to uninstall AdGuard Home;
- `-v` for verbose output.

Note that options `-r` and `-u` are mutually exclusive.

### Alternative methods

#### Manual installation

Please read the **[Getting Started][wiki-start]** article on our Wiki to learn how to install AdGuard Home manually, and how to configure your devices to use it.

#### Docker

You can use our official Docker image on [Docker Hub].

#### Snap Store

If you're running **Linux,** there's a secure and easy way to install AdGuard Home: get it from the [Snap Store].

[Docker Hub]: https://hub.docker.com/r/adguard/adguardhome
[Snap Store]: https://snapcraft.io/adguard-home
[wiki-start]: https://adguard-dns.io/kb/adguard-home/getting-started/

### Guides

See our [Wiki][wiki].

[wiki]: https://github.com/AdguardTeam/AdGuardHome/wiki

### API

If you want to integrate with AdGuard Home, you can use our [REST API][openapi]. Alternatively, you can use this [python client][pyclient], which can be used to build the [AdGuard Home Assistant integration][assistant-integration].

[assistant-integration]:   https://www.home-assistant.io/integrations/adguard/
[openapi]:  https://github.com/AdguardTeam/AdGuardHome/tree/master/openapi
[pyclient]: https://pypi.org/project/adguardhome/

## Comparing AdGuard Home to other solutions

### How is this different from public AdGuard DNS servers?

Running your own AdGuard Home server allows you to do much more than using a public DNS server. It's a completely different level. See for yourself:

- Choose what exactly the server blocks and permits.

- Monitor your network activity.

- Add your own custom filtering rules.

- **Most importantly, it's your own server, and you are the only one who's in control.**

### How does AdGuard Home compare to Pi-Hole

At this point, AdGuard Home has a lot in common with Pi-Hole. Both block ads and trackers using the so-called “DNS sinkholing” method and both allow customizing what's blocked.

> [!NOTE]
> We're not going to stop here. DNS sinkholing is not a bad starting point, but this is just the beginning.

AdGuard Home provides a lot of features out-of-the-box with no need to install and configure additional software. We want it to be simple to the point when even casual users can set it up with minimal effort.

> [!NOTE]
> Some of the listed features can be added to Pi-Hole by installing additional software or by manually using SSH terminal and reconfiguring one of the utilities Pi-Hole consists of. However, in our opinion, this cannot be legitimately counted as a Pi-Hole's feature.

| Feature                                                                 | AdGuard Home | Pi-Hole                                                   |
|-------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------|
| Blocking ads and trackers                                               | ✅                | ✅                                                        |
| Customizing blocklists                                                  | ✅                | ✅                                                        |
| Built-in DHCP server                                                    | ✅                | ✅                                                        |
| HTTPS for the Admin interface                                           | ✅                | Kind of, but you'll need to manually configure lighttpd   |
| Encrypted DNS upstream servers (DNS-over-HTTPS, DNS-over-TLS, DNSCrypt) | ✅                | ❌ (requires additional software)                         |
| Cross-platform                                                          | ✅                | ❌ (not natively, only via Docker)                        |
| Running as a DNS-over-HTTPS or DNS-over-TLS server                      | ✅                | ❌ (requires additional software)                         |
| Blocking phishing and malware domains                                   | ✅                | ❌ (requires non-default blocklists)                      |
| Parental control (blocking adult domains)                               | ✅                | ❌ (requires non-default blocklists)                      |
| Force Safe search on search engines                                     | ✅                | ❌                                                        |
| Per-client (device) configuration                                       | ✅                | ✅                                                        |
| Access settings (choose who can use AGH DNS)                            | ✅                | ❌                                                        |
| Running [without root privileges][wiki-noroot]                          | ✅                | ❌                                                        |

[wiki-noroot]: https://adguard-dns.io/kb/adguard-home/getting-started/#running-without-superuser

### How does AdGuard Home compare to traditional ad blockers

It depends.

DNS sinkholing is capable of blocking a big percentage of ads, but it lacks the flexibility and the power of traditional ad blockers. You can get a good impression about the difference between these methods by reading [this article][blog-adaway], which compares AdGuard for Android (a traditional ad blocker) to hosts-level ad blockers (which are almost identical to DNS-based blockers in their capabilities). This level of protection is enough for some users.

Additionally, using a DNS-based blocker can help to block ads, tracking and analytics requests on other types of devices, such as SmartTVs, smart speakers or other kinds of IoT devices (on which you can't install traditional ad blockers).

### Known limitations

Here are some examples of what cannot be blocked by a DNS-level blocker:

- YouTube, Twitch ads;

- Facebook, Twitter, Instagram sponsored posts.

Essentially, any advertising that shares a domain with content cannot be blocked by a DNS-level blocker.

Is there a chance to handle this in the future?  DNS will never be enough to do this. Our only option is to use a content blocking proxy like what we do in the standalone AdGuard applications. We're [going to bring][issue-1228] this feature support to AdGuard Home in the future. Unfortunately, even in this case, there still will be cases when this won't be enough or would require quite a complicated configuration.

[blog-adaway]: https://adguard.com/blog/adguard-vs-adaway-dns66.html
[issue-1228]:  https://github.com/AdguardTeam/AdGuardHome/issues/1228

## How to build from source

### Prerequisites

Run `make init` to prepare the development environment.

You will need this to build AdGuard Home:

- [Go](https://golang.org/dl/) v1.25 or later;
- [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/en/download/) v24.10.0 or later;
- [npm](https://www.npmjs.com/) v10.8 or later;

### Building

Open your terminal and execute these commands:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/AdguardTeam/AdGuardHome
cd AdGuardHome
make
```

> [!WARNING]
> The non-standard `-j` flag is currently not supported, so building with `make -j 4` or setting your `MAKEFLAGS` to include, for example, `-j 4` is likely to break the build. If you do have your `MAKEFLAGS` set to that, and you don't want to change it, you can override it by running `make -j 1`.

Check the [`Makefile`][src-makefile] to learn about other commands.

#### Building for a different platform

You can build AdGuard Home for any OS/ARCH that Go supports. In order to do this, specify `GOOS` and `GOARCH` environment variables as macros when running `make`.

For example:

```sh
env GOOS='linux' GOARCH='arm64' make
```

or:

```sh
make GOOS='linux' GOARCH='arm64'
```

#### Preparing releases

You'll need [`snapcraft`] to prepare a release build. Once installed, run the following command:

```sh
make build-release CHANNEL='...' VERSION='...'
```

See the [`build-release` target documentation][targ-release].

#### Docker image

Run `make build-docker` to build the Docker image locally (the one that we publish to DockerHub). Please note, that we're using [Docker Buildx][buildx] to build our official image.

You may need to prepare before using these builds:

- (Linux-only) Install Qemu:

  ```sh
  docker run --rm --privileged multiarch/qemu-user-static --reset -p yes --credential yes
  ```

- Prepare the builder:

  ```sh
  docker buildx create --name buildx-builder --driver docker-container --use
  ```

See the [`build-docker` target documentation][targ-docker].

#### Debugging the frontend

When you need to debug the frontend without recompiling the production version every time, for example to check how your labels would look on a form, you can run the frontend build a development environment.

1. In a separate terminal, run:

   ```sh
   ( cd ./client/ && env NODE_ENV='development' npm run watch )
   ```

2. Run your `AdGuardHome` binary with the `--local-frontend` flag, which instructs AdGuard Home to ignore the built-in frontend files and use those from the `./build/` directory.

3. Now any changes you make in the `./client/` directory should be recompiled and become available on the web UI. Make sure that you disable the browser cache to make sure that you actually get the recompiled version.

## pi-hole/pi-hole (https://github.com/pi-hole/pi-hole)
Description: A black hole for Internet advertisements
Homepage: https://pi-hole.net
Language: Shell; license: NOASSERTION; created 2014-06-08; last push 2026-11-15
Latest release: v6.6 (2026-11-11)
README (start):
#

  
  
  Network-wide ad blocking via your own Linux hardware

The Pi-hole® is a [DNS sinkhole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DNS_Sinkhole) that protects your devices from unwanted content without installing any client-side software.

- **Easy-to-install**: our dialogs walk you through the simple installation process in less than ten minutes
- **Resolute**: content is blocked in _non-browser locations_, such as ad-laden mobile apps and smart TVs
- **Responsive**: seamlessly speeds up the feel of everyday browsing by caching DNS queries
- **Lightweight**: runs smoothly with [minimal hardware and software requirements](https://docs.pi-hole.net/main/prerequisites/)
- **Robust**: a command-line interface that is quality assured for interoperability
- **Insightful**: a beautiful responsive Web Interface dashboard to view and control your Pi-hole
- **Versatile**: can optionally function as a [DHCP server](https://discourse.pi-hole.net/t/how-do-i-use-pi-holes-built-in-dhcp-server-and-why-would-i-want-to/3026), ensuring _all_ your devices are protected automatically
- **Scalable**: [capable of handling hundreds of millions of queries](https://pi-hole.net/2017/05/24/how-much-traffic-can-pi-hole-handle/) when installed on server-grade hardware
- **Modern**: blocks ads over both IPv4 and IPv6
- **Free**: open source software that helps ensure _you_ are the sole person in control of your privacy

-----

## One-Step Automated Install

Those who want to get started quickly and conveniently may install Pi-hole using the following command:

```bash
curl -sSL https://install.pi-hole.net | bash
```

## Alternative Install Methods

Piping to `bash` is [controversial](https://pi-hole.net/2016/07/25/curling-and-piping-to-bash), as it prevents you from [reading code that is about to run](https://github.com/pi-hole/pi-hole/blob/master/automated%20install/basic-install.sh) on your system. Therefore, we provide these alternative installation methods which allow code review before installation:

### Method 1: Clone our repository and run

```bash
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/pi-hole/pi-hole.git Pi-hole
cd "Pi-hole/automated install/"
sudo bash basic-install.sh
```

### Method 2: Manually download the installer and run

```bash
wget -O basic-install.sh https://install.pi-hole.net
sudo bash basic-install.sh
```

### Method 3: Using Docker to deploy Pi-hole

Please refer to the [Pi-hole docker repo](https://github.com/pi-hole/docker-pi-hole) to use the Official Docker Images.

## [Post-install: Make your network take advantage of Pi-hole](https://docs.pi-hole.net/main/post-install/)

Once the installer has been run, you will need to [configure your router to have **DHCP clients use Pi-hole as their DNS server**](https://discourse.pi-hole.net/t/how-do-i-configure-my-devices-to-use-pi-hole-as-their-dns-server/245). This router configuration will ensure that all devices connecting to your network will have content blocked without any further intervention.

If your router does not support setting the DNS server, you can [use Pi-hole's built-in DHCP server](https://discourse.pi-hole.net/t/how-do-i-use-pi-holes-built-in-dhcp-server-and-why-would-i-want-to/3026); be sure to disable DHCP on your router first (if it has that feature available).

As a last resort, you can manually set each device to use Pi-hole as their DNS server.

There are many reoccurring costs involved with maintaining free, open-source, and privacy-respecting software; expenses which [our volunteer developers](https://github.com/orgs/pi-hole/people) pitch in to cover out-of-pocket. ## https://raw.githubusercontent.com/paimonsoror/telltaledns/main/deploy/compose/compose.yaml
URL: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/paimonsoror/telltaledns/main/deploy/compose/compose.yaml

# TelltaleDNS on a Raspberry Pi (or any Linux box) with Docker Compose (REQ: OPS-004, spec/08 §3.4).
#
#   docker compose up -d
#   docker compose exec telltale telltale auth setup-token   # then open http://<pi>:8053/
#
# Host networking: queries keep the real client addresses and the neighbor table shows
# MAC addresses, so per-device statistics and rules work. Nothing else may use port 53 on
# the host (see README.md for systemd-resolved).
name: telltale
services:
  telltale:
    image: ghcr.io/paimonsoror/telltale:${TELLTALE_TAG:-latest}
    command: ["run", "-c", "/etc/telltale/telltale.toml"]
    network_mode: host
    restart: unless-stopped
    # Port 53 needs NET_BIND_SERVICE: run as root with only that capability. To run as the
    # image's unprivileged user instead, set the host sysctl net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start=53
    # (README.md) and uncomment `user`.
    user: "0:0"
    # user: "65532:65532"
    cap_drop: [ALL]
    cap_add: [NET_BIND_SERVICE]
    security_opt: ["no-new-privileges:true"]
    read_only: true
    volumes:
      - ./telltale.toml:/etc/telltale/telltale.toml:ro
      # Lists, the query log, users. Docker creates ./data owned by root; when switching to the
      # unprivileged user, first run `sudo chown -R 65532:65532 data`.
      - ./data:/var/lib/telltale
    environment:
      TELLTALE_LOG: info
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "/usr/local/bin/telltale", "health", "--url", "http://127.0.0.1:8053/readyz"]
      interval: 30s
      timeout: 5s
      start_period: 30s
    logging:
      driver: json-file
      options: { max-size: "10m", max-file: "3" }

## https://raw.githubusercontent.com/paimonsoror/telltaledns/main/deploy/compose/telltale.toml
URL: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/paimonsoror/telltaledns/main/deploy/compose/telltale.toml

# TelltaleDNS starter config (REQ: OPS-004) — the same file the Compose bundle and install.sh use.
# Every key is optional; see docs/configuration.md. Check edits with:
#   telltale config check /etc/telltale/telltale.toml
# Changes apply on reload (SIGHUP / `docker compose kill -s HUP`) without dropping queries.
config_version = 1

# DNS listens on UDP and TCP port 53 on every address (IPv4 and IPv6) unless [[listen]] is
# set. The web UI and API listen on port 8053: open http://<this machine>:8053/ and use the
# setup token from `telltale auth setup-token` (Compose: `docker compose exec telltale
# telltale auth setup-token`) to create the first admin.

# Where answers come from: encrypted (DNS over TLS) to Cloudflare and Quad9, whichever is
# faster. `telltale presets list` shows other providers.
[[upstream]]
name = "cloudflare"
url = "tls://1.1.1.1:853"
tls_server_name = "cloudflare-dns.com"

[[upstream]]
name = "quad9"
url = "tls://9.9.9.9:853"
tls_server_name = "dns.quad9.net"

[[upstream_group]]
name = "default"
members = ["cloudflare", "quad9"]
strategy = "fastest"

# A balanced ad and tracker blocklist (about 150k names), refreshed daily.
[[list]]
name = "hagezi-pro"
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hagezi/dns-blocklists/main/adblock/pro.txt"

# On an SD-card Pi, keep the query log small (or put /var/lib/telltale on a USB SSD).
[telemetry.qlog]
retention_days = 7

## FAQ — TelltaleDNS
URL: https://paimonsoror.github.io/telltaledns/faq.html
Description: Answers to what people ask most about TelltaleDNS: replacing Pi-hole or Unbound, resolving from the root servers, blocking categories, per-device encrypted DNS, high availability, and running on Kubernetes.

Skip to content
TelltaleDNS
☰
◐

QUESTIONS PEOPLE ASK

FAQ

Short answers, each with a link to the details. Missing yours? Open an issue and it may end up here.

Is it right for me?
Resolving names
Blocking
Devices and encrypted DNS
Clusters and availability
Monitoring
Is it right for me?
Is it a replacement for Pi-hole or AdGuard Home with Unbound?

Yes, it can replace that combination. It filters with blocklists and per-device groups, and it can also resolve names itself from the root servers, so there is no second program to run.

Two things to know. There is no DHCP server (below), and the importers cover Pi-hole (telltale import pihole) and Technitium but not AdGuard Home, so you would add those lists again. Lists written in AdGuard syntax work as they are. Upgrades, backups, and moving in walks through it.

Can I run it next to my existing DNS server instead of replacing it?

Yes. Point your devices at TelltaleDNS and add your current server as an upstream, or send only some domains to it (conditional forwarding), or point your current server's forwarder at TelltaleDNS. When you want to move zones across, zone files import. See Encrypted DNS and upstreams.

What is it good at?

Three things it was built around:

Explaining. The query log says why each question was answered or blocked, which list and rule did it, and which upstream answered.
Trying before you commit. You can run a new list or rule against yesterday's real traffic and see what it would have blocked before you save it. See Change things safely.
Seeing. Per-device and per-group statistics, service-level objectives, and Prometheus metrics. See the tour of the web UI.
Does it include a DHCP server?

No, on purpose. DHCP stays on your router or another server. TelltaleDNS reads device names from your router's lease list (UniFi and OPNsense) and from mDNS, so devices still show up by name. See how devices get their names.

Is it a firewall or a network monitor?

No. It sees DNS lookups and only those: which devices ask for which names, and what happened to each question. It needs nothing installed on the devices, and it sits comfortably next to a firewall or an endpoint monitor, which watch different things.

Who builds it, and will it be maintained?

One maintainer builds it and runs it at home. It is free and open source, under either the Apache 2.0 or the MIT license, and the aim is community-driven development as it grows. Issues, pull requests, and ideas are welcome, and everyone who contributes is credited in the README.

It is developed with Claude Code, and every commit it worked on carries a Co-Authored-By: Claude line. The README says so under Built with Claude.

Resolving names
Can it resolve from the root servers instead of Quad9, Cloudflare, or another public resolver?

Yes. Use a recursive:// upstream:

[[upstream]]
name = "recursive"
url = "recursive://"

[[upstream_group]]
name = "default"
members = ["recursive"]

No public resolver then sees your lookups. Each server is asked only as much of the name as it needs (so the root servers see com, not the whole name), answers can be checked with DNSSEC, and delegations are remembered, so only the first lookup in a new zone takes a few round trips.

The trade-off: the authoritative servers see your address, and your ISP still sees the traffic. You can mix it with a forwarder as a fallback in a failover group. Details: recursive resolution.

My domain's servers are authoritative-only (BIND with recursion off, NSD, Knot). How do I send the domain to them?

Use a stub zone. In Names on my network → Send a domain to another server, tick These servers only know this domain (or set stub_zone and stub_servers on a recursive:// upstream). Names under the domain then start at those servers, without asking them to recurse, and delegations to sub-domains are followed. Health checks ask the zone's SOA instead of . NS, which servers like these refuse. Details: stub zones.

Can it serve my own names and zones?

Yes, at two levels. Local records answer single names (A, AAAA, CNAME, PTR, TXT, MX, SRV, with wildcards), and PTR records for your A and AAAA records are made for you. Local zones make TelltaleDNS the authority for a whole domain, from an RFC 1035 zone file or written inline, and a zone can be limited to some groups for split-horizon DNS. Manage them in the web UI or the API, or import a zone export with telltale import zone.

It is built for home and office zones, not as a public authoritative server: there are no zone transfers or secondary zones. Details: local records and zones.

How do reverse (PTR) lookups of my LAN addresses work?

By default, reverse lookups for private addresses answer NXDOMAIN, so your LAN layout never goes to a public resolver. To resolve them, add records yourself, or send your reverse zone to the server that knows your devices, such as your router:

[[upstream]]
name = "home-router"
url = "udp://192.168.1.1"

[[upstream_group]]
name = "lan"
members = ["home-router"]

[[route]]
match_suffix = ["home.arpa", "168.192.in-addr.arpa"]
upstream_group = "lan"

The same thing is a few clicks in Send a domain to another server.

Can a script add DNS records, for example when a container starts?

Yes. The API takes a record per name:

curl -X PUT -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"records": [{"type": "A", "value": "192.168.1.10"}]}' \
  http://dns.lan:8053/api/v1/records/nas.home.arpa

Add ?dryRun=true to preview a change. Tokens are made in the web UI (Users and sign-in). If your configuration comes from Git, changes go through Git instead and the API refuses them.

Blocking
Does it block ads and security threats?

Yes. Setup offers several starting blocklists, and you can add your own by URL in hosts, plain-domain, wildcard, AdBlock/AdGuard DNS, or Pi-hole regex format. Lists apply per group, and every block says which list and rule caused it. See Block, allow, and explain.

Can I block whole categories, such as adult content?

Not with a single switch, and that is by design: TelltaleDNS never looks at page content, which keeps it fast. Categories come from the people who maintain category blocklists. You can get the same result for just the devices that need it:

Add a category blocklist by URL and give it only to that group.
Send that group to a family-filtering upstream (the presets include several).
Turn on safe search for the group, and block specific services such as TikTok or Roblox with one setting.

A group with no list setting uses every list, so give your other groups an explicit list of the ones they should use.

Devices and encrypted DNS
Can each device use DoH or DoT with its own identity?

Yes. Every encrypted listener (DoT, DoH, DoH over HTTP/3, and DoQ) takes a client ID: use https://dns.example.com/dns-query/kids-tablet, or the name kids-tablet.dns.example.com with a wildcard certificate. Match it in the configuration with [[client]] match = ["id:kids-tablet"], and the device lands in a group with its own lists, schedule, safe search, and upstream. The ID follows the device, even on mobile data.

The ID names a device; it is not a password. Who may ask at all is decided by the sender's address ([access] allowed_networks). If you host it on the internet for phones, put it behind a VPN such as WireGuard or Tailscale (Tailscale's range is allowed by default) or open that setting deliberately. Details: Encrypted DNS and upstreams.

This is one of the newer areas, so reports from real setups are especially welcome.

How does it name my devices?

In order: names you give them, then your router's DHCP leases (UniFi and OPNsense, read through their APIs every few minutes), then the names devices announce over mDNS. Clients → Discovered lists everything found. See Groups, devices, and VLANs.

Two things it doesn't do yet: look up a device's reverse (PTR) record to name it, and accept dynamic DNS updates (RFC 2136) from a DHCP server. Lease and mDNS names label devices in the interface and the query log; they are not served as DNS answers. If you need either, an issue describing your setup helps.

Every query shows the same client address. What's wrong?

Something between your devices and TelltaleDNS rewrites the sender, and the web UI shows a "Client IPs appear masked" banner naming the address. The usual causes and fixes:

A router that forwards DNS: hand out TelltaleDNS's address in DHCP instead. If it has to forward, enable the router's EDNS MAC option (dnsmasq add-mac) and list it in [clients] trust_edns_mac_from.
Kubernetes with externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster: use Local (the chart's default) or hostNetwork: true.
Docker with a proxy or bridge: use network_mode: host.

Details: seeing real client IPs.

Clusters and availability
Does it support high availability, and does the configuration sync?

Yes. Nodes form a cluster with one primary. Its configuration and blocklists reach every node within seconds over an encrypted, mutually authenticated link, every node answers DNS, and every node's dashboard and query log show the whole cluster. Nodes can be different platforms: a Kubernetes node with a Raspberry Pi, two Pis, or several pods. See Build a cluster.

Is it active-active? Does it need an external database?

No external database. Each node keeps its own small embedded store, so there is nothing shared to keep consistent. Answering DNS is active-active: every node, including extra resolver pods, answers queries with the same configuration. Configuration changes go through one primary and are signed and copied to the others.

What happens if the primary, or my Kubernetes cluster, goes down?

DNS keeps working. Every other node keeps answering from the last configuration it received, even after a restart. What pauses is changing the configuration. Promote another eligible node from the Cluster page or with telltale cluster promote, or use automatic failover with a third voter such as a small witness node.

If the configuration comes from Git, a node that isn't Git-managed can only be promoted as an emergency primary, which keeps the cluster on its last version until a Git-managed node is back. Manual promotion is the predictable choice there.

Can a Raspberry Pi be the primary, with the configuration coming from Git?

Yes. Any eligible node that has the same [cluster.git] section can take over and keep following the repository, so the Pi can follow your repository directly while Argo CD or Flux keeps managing the Kubernetes side. Join the Pi with a token made for eligible nodes. Details under "Where configuration comes from" in the cluster documentation.

Isn't DNS in Kubernetes risky when Kubernetes needs DNS itself?

The chart is built around that. TelltaleDNS's own pods keep asking CoreDNS for the cluster's names, so they never depend on their own Service, and you can leave CoreDNS as the second server for your pods, so lookups still work if the TelltaleDNS Service has no ready pods. You can also keep a node outside the cluster, such as a Pi, as a replica, so the rest of the network has DNS even while the cluster is down. See Run on Kubernetes.

Monitoring
Does it have Prometheus metrics, and can I use Grafana?

Yes. /metrics is served on port 9153 by default, limited to your allowed networks. It covers queries per transport, the cache, upstream latency and health, blocks per list and group, and where the time goes inside each answer. The Helm chart has an optional ServiceMonitor, alert rules, and a Grafana dashboard, and metrics can be pushed to an OpenTelemetry collector instead. See Monitoring and alerts.

How do I report a problem without sharing my network?

Make a support package: one file with your build, your settings without secrets, health, upstream state, a metrics snapshot, and the node's recent log. By default every address and name in it is replaced by a pseudonym (device-1, 10.4.7.9) that is the same all through the file, a subnet stays a subnet, and nothi

STANDING ON THE SHOULDERS OF GIANTS

Inspired by Pi-hole and Technitium

TelltaleDNS exists because two projects showed what self-hosted DNS can be. We're grateful to both communities, and if either one already serves you well, keep using it.

Pi-hole

Brought network-wide ad blocking to millions of homes, on a $35 computer, with a dashboard anyone can read. Its blocklist formats, regex rules and Teleporter export are a shared language, and TelltaleDNS reads them as they are.

Technitium DNS Server

Showed how complete a self-hosted DNS server can be: encrypted DNS, real zones, and a capable web console. Its API makes bringing a setup across to TelltaleDNS straightforward.

TelltaleDNS is an independent, clean-room project under Apache-2.0 OR MIT: it uses their public documentation and data formats, not their code.
